restatements.text: Proposes an amendment to the California Constitution by adding Section 4.5 to Article XIII A.

Starting January 1, 2027, prohibits local governments and local voter initiatives from imposing, extending, or increasing any special tax without a two-thirds vote of the electorate, overriding certain other constitutional provisions.
Prohibits local governments and local voter initiatives from imposing ad valorem taxes on real property, with limited existing exceptions.
Defines 'local government' and 'special tax' according to Section 1 of Article XIII C.

evidence.quote: no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax, except as provided in Section 4 of this article, subdivision (d) of Section 2 of Article XIII C, and paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D, unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.
evidence.why: It reduces government taxing power by requiring a two-thirds supermajority for local governments to impose special taxes.

evidence.quote: no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose ad valorem taxes on real property, except as provided in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D.
evidence.why: It reduces government taxing power by banning local governments from imposing ad valorem property taxes.

analysis.answer: Current law was not provided. Based on the measure text alone, it newly adds a requirement that any special tax proposed, extended, or increased by a local government or by voter initiative must be approved by a two-thirds vote, and it constitutionally prohibits local ad valorem property taxes.

Local governments may face revenue constraints and might turn to general taxes, fees, or assessments that require lower approval thresholds. Advocates for special taxes will have to invest more resources to achieve a two-thirds majority or may abandon some efforts entirely.

It addresses the perceived problem of local taxes and property taxes increasing too easily, particularly through local initiatives that might currently only require a simple majority. It may create the problem of local governments being unable to fund desired public services because a minority of voters can block special tax measures.
A minority block of voters (one-third plus one) gains the power to veto special taxes. The state gains power by strictly capping local tax autonomy.

The effect of supermajority requirements on local government revenues and services is empirically studied; researchers generally agree it reduces revenue growth, but debate whether this forces beneficial efficiency and prioritization or causes harmful cuts to essential services.
Because it amends the state constitution, it can only be undone or modified by another statewide ballot measure.
